title: India hosts Agrivoltaics World Conference 2026 for the first time in the Global South
subtitle:
Union Minister of Agriculture and Union Minister for New & Renewable Energy Jointly inaugurates AgriVoltaics World Conference 2026

AgriVoltaics policies must be designed to meet the practical requirements of India’s small and marginal farmers: Shri Chouhan

Next phase of PM KUSUM to further expand solar energy in agriculture sector: Shri Joshi
ministry: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 OCT 2026 5:40PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare of India Shri Shivraj Singh Chouhan and Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy, Education and Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, Shri Pralhad Joshi jointly inaugurated the three days AgriVoltaics World Conference 2026 here today.
The Agriculture Minister while addressing the inaugural session, emphasised that under the leadership of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, farmers could become both
Annadatas
and
Urjadatas
by adopting solar energy alongside farming. Shri Chouhan highlighted that the integration of agriculture and solar power could promote global welfare and enhance farmers’ economic prosperity. He stressed that agrivoltaics policies must be designed to meet the practical requirements of India’s small and marginal farmers, who constitute more than 85 per cent of the farming community.
Shri Chouhan explained that agrivoltaics enables solar power generation through panels installed above agricultural land while allowing crops to grow. He noted that electricity had become indispensable to modern life and agriculture, making the integration of energy generation with farming an important step towards farmers’ welfare.
Highlighting India’s agricultural progress, the Minister recalled that the country was earlier dependent on foodgrain imports to meet its food security requirements. He stated that India’s foodgrain stocks were now well supplied with wheat and rice, reflecting the contribution of farmers. He further noted that the agricultural sector had sustained a growth rate of 4.5 per cent and that agricultural exports had reached a record USD 52.55 billion.
The Union Agriculture Minister drew attention to the structural challenges faced by agriculture sector, noting that the average landholding in the country was only 0.96 hectares. He emphasised that agrivoltaics models must allow farmers to continue cultivation instead of replacing farming with solar power generation.
He called for practical system designs that accounted for panel height, spacing between support structures and the movement of agricultural machinery, enabling farmers to undertake ploughing and change crops and cropping patterns according to their needs.
Shri Chouhan also underscored the need for effective rainwater drainage and harvesting arrangements to prevent soil erosion and ensure the optimal use of water. He further advocated the active involvement of Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) and training for rural youth and women in equipment operation, repair and maintenance to create employment opportunities in villages.
Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Shri Pralhad Joshi while delivering the address highlighted India’s progress in expanding clean energy capacity alongside economic growth. He stated that India’s non-fossil fuel-based installed electricity capacity had reached 308.03 GW, accounting for more than 55 per cent of the country’s total installed electricity capacity of approximately 560 GW.
The New & Renewable Energy Minister highlighted India’s broader economic and technological transformation under the visionary leadership of Hon’ble Prime Minister.
Emphasising the importance of balancing food security, energy requirements and land availability, the Minister described agrivoltaics as an approach that could enable farmers to earn from both cultivation and electricity generation on the same land. He reiterated the principle of “One land, two harvests”.
He quoted a study by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) that estimated 47.5 million hectares, or approximately 30 per cent of India’s 160 million hectares of cropland, were technically suitable for agrivoltaics. One deployment scenario covering 16 million hectares estimated annual electricity generation of 12,775 TWh, potentially comparable to or exceeding India’s projected electricity demand of 5,250–10,020 TWh by 2050. The Minister noted that these were technical estimates and that actual deployment would depend on local conditions and feasibility. Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh together accounted for nearly 50 per cent of India’s estimated agrivoltaic potential.
Shri Joshi highlighted that agrivoltaics could be adapted to different agricultural activities, including fruit and plantation crops, vegetables, spices, horticulture, floriculture and fodder, as well as livestock rearing in suitable settings. He noted that field studies had indicated potential yield improvements of 10–20 per cent for certain crops and reductions of around 30 per cent in water consumption under suitable systems.
The Minister also highlighted the potential to integrate agricultural infrastructure with electricity-grid planning. He noted that more than 7.70 lakh geo-tagged rural facilities had been mapped under the PM Gram Sadak Yojana and that over 400 integrated cold-chain projects had been approved under the PM Kisan SAMPADA Yojana. He suggested that agricultural facility maps could be integrated with grid infrastructure to identify suitable project locations near mandis, warehouses and cold chains, thereby improving logistics and project viability.
Highlighting existing efforts to expand solar energy in agriculture, Shri Joshi noted that PM-KUSUM had supported decentralised solar power plants, standalone solar pumps and the solarisation of existing grid-connected pumps, including feeder-level solarisation. He also highlighted the contribution of decentralised solar capacity, which had reached 16.3 GW during the previous year, comprising 7.6 GW under PM-KUSUM and 8.7 GW under rooftop solar, largely through the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana, which had crossed 63 lakh beneficiaries.
The Minister announced that one of the world’s most ambitious agrivoltaic programmes would be launched under the next phase of PM-KUSUM. He stated that the initiative would provide an opportunity to further expand solar energy in agriculture by aligning the scheme with existing agricultural programmes. He noted that elevated and tilted structures could make agrivoltaic plants 25–30 per cent more expensive than conventional ground-mounted solar installations, and that the government aimed to bridge this cost gap by supporting AgriPV capacity creation.
Shri Joshi observed that the average cost of electricity supply had been around ₹7 per unit in 2025–26, while some agrivoltaic assessments indicated potential generation costs of ₹3.20–₹3.30 per unit under specific assumptions. He highlighted that competitive project designs and financing models could help make agrivoltaics commercially viable.
Referring to international experience, the Minister noted that the global agrivoltaics market had surpassed 18.4 GW of installed capacity in 2025. He highlighted Italy’s €1.7 billion funding programme for farmers, solar developers and research institutions; Japan’s opening of all categories of farmland to agrivoltaics and support for small-scale systems through preferential tariffs; and Germany’s linkage of support to continued agricultural use and minimum crop-yield requirements.
He further highlighted the employment potential of the sector. According to the AgriPV Manual of the Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy, agrivoltaics could generate between 1.10 lakh and 3.32 lakh full-time-equivalent jobs, contributing to agricultural productivity, skills development, entrepreneurship and rural employment.
The Minister emphasised the importance of international partnerships in developing agrivoltaic solutions suited to the needs of the Global South. He acknowledged the contributions of German partners, the Indo-German Cooperation on Agrivoltaics, the International Solar Alliance and other institutions working to advance the sector. He noted that countries across Africa, Asia and Latin America faced common challenges relating to smallholder farmers, water stress, reliable clean energy and affordable technologies, and called for cooperation based on mutual learning and locally adapted solutions.
Shri Joshi highlighted the launch of the Global Agrivoltaics Climate-Zone Technical Framework as an important step towards wider adoption of the technology. The framework was intended to support governments, farmers, developers, researchers and financiers in making informed decisions, establishing technical standards and moving from isolated pilot projects towards broader implementation.
Secretary, Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Shri Santosh Kumar Sarangi highlighted the contribution of PM-KUSUM in promoting solar energy in agriculture. He stated that approximately 25 lakh pump sets had been solarised under the programme, benefiting around 25 lakh farmers by enabling them to replace diesel-powered pumps with solar-powered alternatives. He also highlighted the programme’s contribution to reducing diesel consumption and foreign exchange expenditure on crude oil imports.
Shri Sarangi noted that the Ministry was working with the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare to develop the next phase of PM-KUSUM with a broader focus on farmers’ progress, income generation and improved livelihoods. He emphasised the importance of partnerships with international and national institutions and highlighted ongoing efforts to develop appropriate electricity procurement models involving power distribution companies and state energy departments to support agrivoltaics at scale.
Present during the opening ceremony were Shri Shripad Yesso Naik, Minister of State for New & Renewable Energy and Power and Secretary Agriculture and Farmers Welfare of India, Shri Atish Chandra and others. The three days world conference will conclude on 23rd October, 2026.

title: Pulsing signals reveal hidden structure around a famous neutron star
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 OCT 2026 4:46PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Scientists have discovered that one of the brightest X-ray pulsars, Centaurus X-3 is gobbling up material through an accretion disk, which is rare for pulsars of its kind.
The study will not only have implications in developing better-informed models of
the system, which is one of the most widely studied binary pulsars
that has drawn the attention of scientists because of its intense brightness, but also lead to enhanced understanding of binary pulsars in general.
An X-ray binary pulsar consists of a pulsar— a highly magnetised neutron star, and a Sun-like star bound in a gravitational dance. A neutron star
is a celestial body with the mass of our sun crunched into a ball the size of Bangalore.
In an X-ray binary, the pulsar’s extreme gravity pulls in material ejected by its companion star, and the pulsar starts accreting material from it, shooting out X-rays in the process.
Centaurus X-3, a high-mass X-ray binary (HMXB) where the companion is more than 10 times the Sun’s mass,
was one of the first X-ray pulsars to be discovered, and the third X-ray source to be discovered in the constellation Centaurus, 24000 light years away.
Pulsars emit radiation from their magnetic poles, known as the primary emission. As the pulsar spins, this radiation sweeps past any satellite waiting to detect it. This radiation also falls around the neutron star. Structures in its wider environment (such as the pulsar’s surface, the surface of its companion star, stellar wind blown out from the companion star), absorb and re-emit this radiation, which scientists call the secondary radiation. Studying these structures is important to understand the system’s physical parameters, such as its orientation and magnetic field strength, leading to enhanced understanding of binary pulsars.
Fig 1
. An artistic impression of the high-mass X-ray binary system Centaurus X-3. Not to scale.
The problem in studying these intricate structures is that X-ray binaries are so distant that they appear as point sources. The secondary radiation is a promising tool to study these structures.
Earlier studies have found that the intensity of secondary emission lines varied with pulsar rotation. Now scientists from the Raman Research Institute (RRI),
an autonomous institution of the Department of Science and
Technology (DST),
led by Kinjal Roy, researcher at RRI, investigated four secondary emission lines in depth and found that
the structure responsible for the varying lines must be co-rotating with the pulsar.
Like a sleuth trying to deduce facts from observational evidence, Roy detected that it is the accretion stream, which is a structure that channels material from the accretion disk towards the pulsar, that is causing the variability in the secondary emission lines.
An accretion stream can exist only if there’s an accretion disk. The accretion stream ushers material from the accretion disk, which gets funnelled into the pulsar’s poles following its magnetic lines. When the accretion stream obscures the satellite’s view of the pulsar while rotating, the primary emission from the pulsar decreases and the secondary emission from the accretion stream increases.
So, accretion in this system occurs through an accretion disk, which is rare in high-mass binaries. In HMXBs, accretion in general happens through direct capture of stellar wind.
“Accretion disk is not expected to occur in [HMXBs] So, if an accretion disk is forming in this system, emission models have to be modified,” says Roy. “When Centaurus X-3 modelling happens in future work, emission from the disk must be accounted for,” he added.
Fig 2
. The accretion stream falling onto the neutron star along its magnetic field lines.

The initiative seeks to complement financial and developmental support with market-oriented interventions, enabling artisans to translate their traditional skills and craftsmanship into viable livelihood opportunities, the official said.
It is pertinent to mention that through initiatives such as Shilp Samagam Mela, the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment continues to advance its efforts towards the socio-economic empowerment of communities having financial constraints, by promoting entrepreneurship, facilitating market access and supporting sustainable livelihoods.

title: Union MoS Raksha Khadse, Guest of Honour at Chhattisgarh Hockey League Opening Ceremony, Calls It a Major Step Towards Strengthening Grassroots Hockey
subtitle: Following Khelo India Tribal Games, Chhattisgarh Hockey League marks another sporting milestone for the state; inaugural edition features six franchises and 132 players
ministry: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 OCT 2026 9:21PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of State for Youth Affairs & Sports Smt. Raksha Khadse was the Guest of Honour at the opening ceremony of the inaugural Chhattisgarh Hockey League (CHL) at the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Hockey Stadium in Raipur on Wednesday, October 21, 2026.
On Building Sporting Momentum in Chhattisgarh
Following the Khelo India Tribal Games, the Chhattisgarh Hockey League marks another significant sporting milestone in the state’s journey towards becoming a stronger sporting hub. While the Khelo India Tribal Games showcased the sporting talent of tribal communities, the league builds on this momentum by creating a dedicated platform for hockey players, strengthening grassroots competition and expanding opportunities for young athletes. Together, these initiatives reflect Chhattisgarh’s growing commitment to sports development and its potential to make a greater contribution to India’s sporting future.
Organised by the Department of Sports and Youth Welfare, Government of Chhattisgarh, and sanctioned by Hockey India, the league brings together six franchise-based teams representing different regions of the state. The inaugural season will run from 21 October to 1 November 2026 at the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Hockey Stadium, Raipur.
On Strengthening Grassroots Hockey
Addressing the occasion, Union MoS Raksha Khadse highlighted the importance of creating structured sporting opportunities for young athletes and strengthening sports development at the grassroots. She emphasised that leagues such as the Chhattisgarh Hockey League can help bridge the gap between grassroots participation and higher levels of competition by enabling young players to compete alongside experienced national and international talent.
She underscored that developing sporting talent requires sustained efforts across the entire ecosystem, including quality coaching, competitive opportunities, sports infrastructure and institutional support. Providing young athletes with the right platforms to demonstrate their abilities is essential to building a stronger sporting culture and expanding India’s talent pool.
Union MoS Raksha Khadse also highlighted the importance of strengthening sports participation among youth in tribal and rural regions. Chhattisgarh has significant potential to contribute to India’s sporting future, and initiatives that connect local talent with established athletes can help young players gain experience, confidence and exposure to higher standards of competition.
On Cultural Identity and Celebrations
The league features six teams: Rajdhani Royals, Nyayadhani Knights, Sanskardhani Strikers, Chakradhar Champions, Bailadila Bulls and Mainpat Titans. Each team comprises 22 players, including 18 players from Chhattisgarh and four players from outside the state. The squads also feature former Olympians as marquee players, bringing experience and competitive quality to the tournament.
A total of 132 players will participate in the inaugural season, including 108 players from Chhattisgarh and 24 guest players. The tournament will feature 18 men’s matches, followed by semi-finals and the final scheduled for 1 November. A women’s exhibition match will also be organised, providing an opportunity to showcase women’s hockey and encourage wider participation in the sport.
Shri Sardar Singh, Olympian and former captain of the Indian hockey team, is the league ambassador. His association with the league is expected to inspire young players and strengthen their connection with India’s hockey legacy.
The league’s identity is rooted in the culture and spirit of Chhattisgarh. Its mascot, Baghwa, draws inspiration from the tiger, while the tagline, “Chalo Re Sangi, Hockey Khelbo”, reflects the local character of the initiative and encourages people across the state to embrace hockey.
The opening ceremony also celebrates Chhattisgarh’s cultural heritage through performances showcasing the state’s traditions, alongside entertainment and sporting tributes. Punjabi singers Jassi Gill and Babbal Rai are among the featured performers.
The tournament offers a total prize pool of ₹21 lakh, with ₹11 lakh for the winning team and ₹6 lakh for the runners-up. Individual awards will also recognise outstanding performances throughout the competition.
All matches will be played at the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Hockey Stadium, Raipur. Entry for spectators is free, and matches will be streamed live on JioHotstar, enabling hockey fans across the country to follow the competition.
The Chhattisgarh Hockey League reflects a broader effort to build a stronger sporting ecosystem by bringing together government support, sporting institutions, experienced athletes and emerging talent. By creating more opportunities for local players to compete and learn, the league seeks to strengthen Chhattisgarh’s contribution to Indian hockey and inspire the next generation of athletes.

title: Transforming Wastewater Treatment
subtitle: Technology and Innovation under Namami Gange
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 OCT 2026 3:46PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Wastewater is generated daily through domestic and urban activities. As towns and cities expand, the volume of sewage requiring collection, conveyance and treatment also increases. Effective treatment therefore requires different technological approaches depending on the nature of sewage, local conditions and available infrastructure. In urban areas, sewage flows through underground networks to centralised treatment plants. However, areas without complete sewer networks require solutions for wastewater collected through septic tanks and other on-site systems. Treatment requirements also vary with sewage characteristics, available land, discharge standards and opportunities for treated-water reuse. Addressing these differences needs a combination of conventional treatment systems and innovative technologies suited to specific situations.
This approach shapes the Namami Gange Programme (NGP), launched in 2014. It is an Integrated Conservation Mission with the twin objectives of effective abatement of pollution, conservation and rejuvenation of the National River Ganga. Main pillars of the Namami Gange Programme are Sewerage Treatment Infrastructure, River-Front Development, River-Surface Cleaning, Biodiversity, Afforestation, Public Awareness, Industrial Effluent Monitoring and Ganga Gram.
The programme places sewage treatment infrastructure at the centre of its pollution-abatement work. It combines the development of new treatment capacity, rehabilitation of existing facilities and the adoption of different treatment technologies. The programme has undertaken 199 sewerage infrastructure projects worth an estimated ₹31,327 crore, of which 116 have been completed. These projects aim to create 5,270 million litres per day (MLD) of new sewage treatment plant (STP) capacity, with 2,237 MLD created so far. The programme also targets the rehabilitation of 925 MLD of existing STP capacity, of which 873 MLD has been rehabilitated. These efforts expand treatment capacity while improving the performance of existing infrastructure.
Namami Gange’s Technology-Neutral Approach
The Namami Gange Programme follows a technology-neutral approach, selecting sewage treatment processes according to local requirements. Adopted technologies include the Conventional Activated Sludge Process, Upflow Anaerobic Sludge Blanket (and its combinations with aerated lagoons), Sequential Batch Reactor, Moving Bed Biofilm Reactor, Fluidized Aerated Bed, and Food Chain Reactor. Other solutions include electrocoagulation, constructed wetlands and packaged systems such as Johkasou.
Activated sludge refers to a mass of microorganisms cultivated in the treatment process to break down organic matter into carbon dioxide, water, and other inorganic compounds.
Sequential Batch Reactor is a cyclic activated sludge treatment process which provides the highest treatment efficiency possible in a single-step biological process.
This flexibility allows treatment infrastructure to address varied conditions, including large urban centres, small habitations, hilly terrain and land-constrained locations. The programme also incorporates innovations such as NEREDA, Soil Biotechnology, on-site Advanced Oxidation Process-based treatment, multi-storey STPs and decentralised systems. Faecal sludge and septage management further extends treatment options beyond conventional sewerage networks.
Food Chain Reactor and Electrocoagulation
Food Chain Reactor
Food Chain Reactor (FCR) technology was introduced in India through the NGP. It improves upon the Activated Sludge Process and Sequential Batch Reactor by incorporating fixed artificial media and plant roots. Its advantages include a smaller footprint, lower power consumption and nutrient removal. The programme records five operational FCR-based STPs: two at Bhatpara, West Bengal and three at Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh. Another plant at Bhagalpur in Bihar is under construction, with an approximate area of 175 square metres per MLD.
Electrocoagulation Technology Applied in Uttarakhand
Electrocoagulation and electro-oxidation represent another treatment approach introduced through the programme. Electrocoagulation is a non-biological treatment process that uses electric current and a coagulant metal anode to destabilise suspended and emulsified pollutants. These systems are suited to cold temperatures, hilly terrain and locations with limited access. Such systems have been implemented in Uttarakhand at locations like Badrinath and Chamoli, with 17 installations recorded. These include a 0.05 MLD STP at Police Chowki, a 1.19 MLD plant at Vivekanand Colony and a 1.25 MLD plant at Pokhari Bend. These systems can therefore extend treatment infrastructure to locations where conventional approaches may be difficult to implement.
Onsite Treatment and Multi-Storey STPs
The programme has also explored treatment solutions that can work closer to the source of wastewater. An Advanced Oxidation Process-based pilot at Varanasi’s Assi Drain was designed to treat excess wastewater onsite, avoiding long interception and diversion sewer lines. The approach uses systems with minimum civil infrastructure and faster execution. Treatment intends to improve water quality, increase dissolved oxygen, and eliminate odour. The model has an innovative financing arrangement. It links payments to the quantity of treated water and achievement of key performance indicators, with no upfront capital payment. This arrangement connects remuneration with treatment performance while allowing freedom in design and configuration.
Another example is the multi-storey sewage treatment plant at Muni Ki Reti, Chandreshwar Nagar. It is the country’s first four-storey STP for a municipality built under the NGP. Limited land, three sewage drains, a stormwater drain and the site’s location upstream of Rishikesh’s Triveni Ghat made conventional construction challenging. The 7.5 MLD plant occupies approximately 900 square metres, using vertical construction to overcome space constraints. Its land requirement is around 120 square metres per MLD with biological nutrient removal, compared with 400 square metres per MLD for the cited conventional alternative. These examples show how treatment design can adapt to site conditions while meeting wastewater-management requirements.
Multi-Storey Sewage Treatment Plant at Muni Ki Reti
Nature-Based and Decentralised Treatment Solutions
Constructed Wetland Treatment
Not every settlement requires the same scale of sewerage infrastructure. In smaller habitations, conventional networks and sewage treatment plants can be expensive, while limited land creates additional challenges. Under NGP, decentralised and nature-based solutions offer alternatives suited to such locations. Constructed wetlands (CWs) are engineered systems that use natural processes to remove pollutants under controlled conditions. A CW system comprises water, plants, growing media (substrate), soil and microorganisms.
Bithoor in Uttar Pradesh demonstrates this approach. With a population of approximately 20,000, the Nagar Panchayat faced high costs for conventional sewerage infrastructure and a lack of suitable land for an STP. Constructed wetlands were selected following third-party appraisal as an emerging treatment technology. Six wetlands were developed directly on drains, providing in-situ treatment for approximately 2 MLD. This resulted in declining Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) levels from around 75 mg/l at the inlet to below 10 mg/l in treated effluent. The technology is considered suitable for drains carrying small, dilute flows where sufficient length and width are available.
Johkasou provides another decentralised option for sewage treatment. It is a packaged treatment facility capable of treating domestic sewage to the desired regulatory and National Green Tribunal (NGT) norms. The system combines several sewage-treatment processes within a prefabricated, plug-and-play unit. Johkasou-based decentralised sewage treatment plants can be useful for low-flow applications, locations where civil construction is difficult and sites with limited space. It also includes locations where systems can be constructed underground. The systems have been used at multiple locations in Uttarakhand, with six installations recorded.
The systems reduce the need for full-time operators and daily sludge handling at the site. Multiple configurations, including cylinder-type and capsule-type options, cater to different flow requirements. Depending on the configuration, the treatment process includes screening, primary treatment, biological treatment, secondary settling, recirculation, disinfection and filtration. These features make Johkasou relevant to settlements where traditional sewerage infrastructure is difficult to build or supervise. Its use in Uttarakhand reflects the need to adapt decentralised sanitation solutions to local geography.
NEREDA: Efficient Biological Treatment
NEREDA is another biological wastewater treatment technology introduced through the NGP which uses aerobic granular sludge. It uses the same bacteria as conventional activated sludge but forms compact aerobic granules with good settling properties. The technology offers a smaller footprint, lower construction costs and reduced operating expenditure. It has also demonstrated power savings of approximately 50% compared with the Activated Sludge Process and 20% compared with the Sequential Batch Reactor (SBR).
A 60 MLD NEREDA-based STP at Pahadi Patna represents these advantages. Its bioreactor occupies approximately 1,900 square metres, compared with 5,400 square metres for the cited SBR bioreactor requirement. NEREDA shows how advanced biological treatment can reduce space and energy requirements in larger installations.
NEREDA Reactor
Soil Biotechnology and Faecal Sludge & Septage Management
Soil Biotechnology-based STP at Devprayag
Soil Biotechnology provides a natural-treatment approach under the programme. This terrestrial wastewater-treatment system combines physical processes such as sedimentation and infiltration with biochemical processes. This removes suspended solids and organic and inorganic contents from wastewater. The system uses a suitable mineral constitution, native microflora, and bio-indicator plants as key components.
Also described as a Constructed Soil Filter, it can be built using Reinforced Cement Concrete (RCC), stone masonry, or soil bunds. Its elements include a raw-water tank, bioreactor containment, treated-water tank, piping and pumps. Depending on the desired water quality, the process can operate as a single-stage or multistage system. The approach minimises mechanical or moving equipment and facilitates easier operation. At Devprayag, a 1.2 MLD Soil Biotechnology-based STP was constructed, with effluent standards based on NGT parameters.
Faecal Sludge and Septage Management addresses another part of the sanitation chain. At Chunar, Uttar Pradesh, a 10 kilolitres per day (KLD) Faecal Sludge Treatment Plant (FSTP) pilot was sanctioned at a construction cost of ₹2.70 crore. Conventional interception and diversion networks and an STP were considered unfeasible due to high costs for the small habitation. Septic tanks and soak pits were prevalent, while drain flows remained low and some drains dried up. Following third-party appraisal, constructed wetlands or other nature-based solutions were identified as more suitable.
An FSTP does not replace an STP, as it treats periodic septage generated from soak pits. Co-processing enables septage from unconnected areas to enter the wider treatment system. It involves a receiving station for septage tankers and transferring the collected material into the network for treatment alongside city sewage.
Faecal Sludge and Septage Management
Energy Recovery, Sludge Management and Resource Use
Under Namami Gange, interventions focus on sludge management, energy recovery and reducing operational and resource requirements. Biogas generation through anaerobic digestion of sludge offers an opportunity for energy recovery. Anaerobic Digestion is the biological degradation of organic matter in the absence of oxygen. The biogas can be used for power generation. Varanasi’s 140 MLD Dinapur STP records an actual flow of approximately 110 MLD and actual total power consumption of 4,20,000 units per month. Biogas-based generation reached around 2,20,000–3,00,000 units monthly, representing approximately 52% to 72%. At the 80 MLD Naini STP in Prayagraj, biogas generation accounted for around 50% of daily power consumption. Other examples include projects at Jajmau in Kanpur and Bhagalpur, while a 220 MLD STP at Meerut is identified for Bio-CNG generation.
Sludge dewatering also contributes to operational efficiency. Dewatering is the separation of solids and liquids to increase the solid content of sludge by removing a portion of the liquid fraction. Volute Press (a sludge-dewatering device) was introduced at the 50 MLD Ramana STP to meet guaranteed energy-consumption and land requirements. Its energy efficiency and compact footprint have prompted consideration of replication. Together, these interventions extend wastewater management beyond pollutant removal to include residual sludge treatment and more efficient plant operation.
Green STPs: Energy Efficiency and Sustainable Operation
The long-term performance of sewage treatment plants depends on treatment standards, efficient operation and sustainable resource use. Under Namami Gange, several initiatives promote green and energy-efficient STPs.
Onsite Solar Power at an STP
On-site solar power was initially introduced at the 42 MLD Naini STP to comply with guaranteed energy consumption. Its 1,000 KW solar plant generates approximately 3,850 units daily against a requirement of 5,700 units. At the 80 MLD Naini STP, solar generation contributes around 1,400 units daily, while biogas supplies another 4,500 units against a total requirement of about 8,900 units. Other installations and projects include the 16 MLD Jhunsi and 14 MLD Phaphamau STPs, alongside projects at Bareilly, Bhagwanpur, Vrindavan, Hathras, Shamli and Saharanpur.
A 220 MLD Meerut STP has also been proposed as a Green STP, with 100% solar power envisaged for the plant and associated facilities. A 10 MW offsite solar plant was being considered by the concessionaire, with electricity supply proposed under the Government of India’s Open Access Policy.
Sludge treatment also contributes to sustainability. A sludge incineration pilot at Rishikesh explores thermal stabilisation and volume reduction. Dewatered municipal sludge containing about 20% solids can be dried to around 90% solids using hot air. The dried sludge is then oxidised in a hot-air generator. The resulting dry ash is not bio-manure, but stabilised ash can be considered for making fire bricks or concrete. At Muni Ki Reti, the pilot was intended to address sludge disposal challenges arising from limited land availability. Together, these efforts combine renewable energy, efficient equipment and improved sludge management to strengthen the environmental and operational sustainability of STPs.
Sludge Treatment at Muni Ki Reti
Rehabilitation, Trunk Sewers and Long-Term Performance
Creating new treatment capacity must be complemented by rehabilitating existing STPs and trunk sewers. Ageing equipment, non-compliance with treatment standards and missing tertiary-treatment components can necessitate upgrades. Under Namami Gange, rehabilitation works address these issues across multiple locations. Examples include the 80 MLD Naini STP in Prayagraj, with electro-mechanical works, biogas power and OCEMS. The 130 MLD Jajmau STP in Kanpur received civil and electro-mechanical rehabilitation, biogas power, chlorination and OCEMS.
Trunk sewer rehabilitation is similarly critical as it addresses siltation, damage and punctures in ageing networks. In Varanasi, a 7-km old brick trunk sewer, up to 2,400 mm in diameter, was taken up using a Glass Reinforced Pipe liner. In Kanpur, 9.3 km of old brick trunk sewer, up to 2,250 mm in diameter, was taken up using Machine Wound Spiral Lining.
The programme also uses the Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM)- based Public-Private Partnership (PPP) and One City/Cluster–One Operator model to integrate new and existing sewage infrastructure. Construction-linked payments are combined with performance-linked payments over 15 years, promoting accountability and sustained operation. Under this model, 31 projects covering 1,955 MLD were taken up. Of these, 11 projects covering 454 MLD have been completed, while 6 projects covering 235 MLD are in an advanced stage of completion. The focus on rehabilitation, operation and maintenance makes wastewater treatment a continuing service rather than a one-time infrastructure activity.
From Sewage Treatment to Sustainable Wastewater Management
Namami Gange’s approach to wastewater treatment combines infrastructure, diverse technologies, decentralised solutions, rehabilitation and long-term operation. Conventional and advanced treatment processes, nature-based systems and emerging technologies address varied local requirements. Performance-based operational models, resource recovery, energy efficiency, sludge management and treated-water reuse strengthen the overall treatment framework. Ultimately, the objective extends beyond building STPs to creating sustainable wastewater-management systems that ensure effective treatment, reliable performance and resource recovery across the river basin.

title: SARAS Mela 2026
subtitle: Taking Rural Women’s Enterprises to the National Markets
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 OCT 2026 11:11AM by PIB Delhi
content:
The SARAS Melas organized under the Centre's
DAY-NRLM
connect rural women entrepreneurs with wider markets, buyers, and business opportunities. The Vijayawada edition marks the
first National SARAS Mela outside Delhi-NCR
, bringing together women entrepreneurs from 34 states and UTs. The platform strengthens DAY-NRLM’s efforts to promote sustainable livelihoods and supports the
Lakhpati Didi
vision of income growth.
Dedicated pavilions
offer opportunities for business learning, institutional support, and enterprise development. Digital platforms like
eSARAS
extend market access beyond physical events, helping rural women take their products to wider markets.
Where Rural Enterprise Meets Opportunity
India’s rural economy is rich in traditional skills, crafts and entrepreneurial talent.
Women’s Self-Help Groups (SHGs) help bring this talent into local economies
. Their products range from handlooms and handicrafts to processed foods and other locally made goods. Yet making a product is only the first step. Rural entrepreneurs also need customers, market information, and opportunities to grow.
SARAS
Melas
help bridge this gap by bringing women-led enterprises closer to consumers, buyers, and institutions. Organised by the government under the
Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana - National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM)
, SARAS Melas have evolved over nearly three decades. They are no longer only exhibitions. They offer a space to sell products, understand consumer preferences, build business connections, and explore wider markets.
The National SARAS Mela in
Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh,
marks a new step in this journey as
it is the first National SARAS Mela to be organised outside the Delhi-NCR region.
The event is running from 13 October 2026 to 31 October 2026 at Punnami Ghat, Vijayawada. Around
1,500
women SHG entrepreneurs and Lakhpati Didis from
34 States and UTs
are showcasing their products through
more than 650 stalls
. The Mela features
regional textiles, handicrafts, natural and processed foods
, and other rural products. An
India Food Court
,
cultural showcases,
and
dedicated learning spaces
add to the experience.
The
decentralisation of the National SARAS Mela
reflects a wider development approach: taking national platforms closer to producers and consumers across India. It connects local skills with new markets while supporting the growth of women-led enterprises. This event paves the way for further decentralisation of other national events and is in line with the approach of conducting international events like BRICS and G20 meetings at regional levels.
From Rural Livelihoods to Market Access: The Role of DAY-NRLM
DAY-NRLM is the government’s flagship programme for reducing rural poverty and promoting women’s economic empowerment. It works through SHGs and their federations, while
supporting financial inclusion and sustainable livelihoods
. The Mission helps women access skills, finance, technology and livelihood opportunities. It also strengthens the market ecosystem around women-led enterprises through product visibility, branding and links with physical, digital and institutional markets.
This market connection matters
because enterprise growth depends on more than production. Women need opportunities to sell beyond their immediate communities. They also benefit from feedback, better product presentation, and connections with buyers. SARAS Melas provide a
practical bridge
between these needs and market opportunities. They bring SHG enterprises, consumers, institutional buyers and other stakeholders together. Entrepreneurs can sell directly, study customer preferences and explore partnerships that may continue after the event.
From 65 Beneficiaries to a National Marketplace
The SARAS journey began in
1999
, when the first National SARAS Mela was organised in Delhi with around
65 beneficiaries
. Since then, the platform has expanded to
national, regional, state
and
district
levels. As on date, a total of
117 National SARAS Melas
and
annual sales exceeding ₹
200 crore
have been recorded. States and Union Territories also organise a minimum of two State-level SARAS Melas a year, bringing the
national
average to around 50 events annually
. Regional and district-level events bring selling opportunities closer to local producers. Together, these formats support market discovery, branding, buyer–seller linkages and enterprise development.
Lakhpati Didi: Making Livelihoods More Sustainable
The Lakhpati Didi initiative is an outcome-oriented livelihood initiative under DAY-NRLM. It builds on the network of women organised through SHGs and their federations. Its focus is to help women and their households achieve sustainable income through diversified livelihood opportunities.
A Lakhpati Didi is an SHG member whose household earns at least
₹
1 lakh annually on a sustainable basis
. The assessment covers at least four agricultural seasons and/or business cycles. The initiative received national impetus in
August
2023
, when the government announced an ambition to create
two crore Lakhpati Didis
. The
target was raised to three crore
in the
Interim Budget 2024-25
. Subsequently, the initiative achieved the
three-crore milestone by December 2025.
In
February 2026
, the government announced an
enhanced target of six crore Lakhpati Didis
. This next phase places greater importance on
sustaining income gains
and helping enterprises grow. Market access, product visibility, branding, and reliable sales channels are important to this effort. SARAS Melas support this transition from livelihood creation to enterprise growth. They can also create opportunities for bulk orders, institutional sales, and longer-term market connections. The Vijayawada Mela brings this connection to life through dedicated spaces for successful entrepreneurs, business learning, and institutional support. Women can share their experience, learn new practices, and explore ways to strengthen their enterprises.
Vijayawada: A National Marketplace with a Regional Reach
The Vijayawada Mela brings products and traditions from across India into one marketplace. Visitors can explore Phulkari from Punjab, Pashmina from Jammu and Kashmir, Ikat and Telia textiles from Telangana, and Paunchei from Mizoram. The stalls also feature Meenakari, Dokra, brasswork, woodcraft and traditional paintings.
A 16-foot installation titled “
SHAKTI - The Spirit of Lakhpati Didi
” forms a signature feature of this Mela. It symbolises the
collective strength of women who preserve traditional craftsmanship
and turn their skills into livelihoods, independence and prosperity.
The Mela is supported by government partners, including the
National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development
(NABARD) and the
National Institute of Rural Development and Panchayati Raj
(NIRDPR). Its design combines direct sales with learning, demonstrations, and connections to institutions. The aim is to make the event useful not only for visitors, but also for the entrepreneurs seeking to build sustainable businesses.
Spaces That Connect Products, Skills and Opportunity
The Vijayawada National SARAS Mela is going beyond a conventional exhibition and retail format by creating a series of
dedicated thematic, knowledge and engagement spaces
. These spaces are providing opportunities for enterprise showcasing, peer learning, knowledge exchange, convergence with government and market stakeholders, live demonstrations, and structured buyer–seller interactions.
Lakhpati Didi Pavilion: Learning from Enterprise Journeys
The Lakhpati Didi Pavilion showcases women who have built successful enterprises. It features entrepreneurs
earning more than ₹
10 lakh annually
,
including women earning over ₹
1 crore
. These women share their journeys, products, business models, and market strategies with other SHG members. Their stories highlight different routes to enterprise growth, including agriculture, non-farm livelihoods, food processing, handicrafts, handlooms and services. Peer learning can help women identify approaches suited to their own skills and circumstances.
Learning and Knowledge Pavilion: Building Business Skills
Strong products need strong business practices. The Learning and Knowledge Pavilion is designed for
workshops, expert talks, masterclasses and experience-sharing sessions
among SHG entrepreneurs, State Rural Livelihood Missions (SRLMs), buyers and other stakeholders. Topics include packaging, branding, preparing business proposals, e-commerce and social media marketing. Further, engagement with public institutions and
private-sector organisations
is also encouraged. These include NABARD, FICCI, CII, ITC, Hindustan Unilever, Amazon and Flipkart. Such interactions can expose entrepreneurs to practical tools for improving product presentation and reaching customers.
Convergence Pavilion: Connecting Women with Support
Growing an enterprise often requires more than market access. Entrepreneurs also need credit, skills, technology, quality certification, and government support. The Convergence Pavilion brings SHG entrepreneurs together with
relevant departments, financial institutions, development agencies and technical institutions
. These organisations and platforms include the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises, Ministry of Textiles, ONDC, Government eMarketplace (GeM) and TRIFED. The pavilion is intended to help women understand relevant schemes, services and support systems.
Demonstration Pavilion: Showing How Products Are Made
A finished product often carries a story of skill, time and technique. The Demonstration Pavilion lets visitors see that process directly. Women entrepreneurs and artisans are
demonstrating live
traditional and contemporary production methods. These activities include
pottery, needlework, and mirror-work embroidery
. Live demonstrations by the Lakhpati Didis create opportunities for practical learning and knowledge exchange. They also help visitors appreciate the craftsmanship behind handmade products, and the
“Demo and Live Learning Area”
offers a special experience.
India Food Court: Regional Flavours and Women’s Enterprise
Food is another route through which rural enterprise reaches consumers. The India Food Court features
50 food stalls
showcasing regional cuisines being prepared in traditional ways using pure spices. The event brings together
more than 200 first-generation women food-service entrepreneurs
from over 28 states and UTs. Visitors can explore street favourites such as Gol Gappe, Chaat and Kebabs. Regional dishes include Litti Chokha from Bihar, Hyderabadi Dum Biryani, Mushroom Pitha from Assam, and Makke Di Roti with Saag from Punjab. Other examples include Vana Sundari from Attappadi in Kerala and Chausela from Chhattisgarh. The food court gives women an opportunity to present regional culinary traditions in a national setting. It also brings the business of food preparation and service into the wider story of women-led entrepreneurship.
Cultural Showcases: Celebrating India’s Diversity
Cultural programmes feature
traditional art forms, crafts, textiles, music and dance
from participating regions, creating an immersive national experience for visitors. These showcases celebrate the heritage behind many of the products on display. They also facilitate participating states in presenting their distinct cultural identities.
Digital Integration: From Physical Stalls to Digital Markets
Digital payments are an important catalyst for business activities at the SARAS Mela.
UPI transactions
support convenient and transparent payments, and the food court primarily operates through cashless transactions. At the same time, keeping in view the convenience of elderly citizens and visitors who may prefer cash payments,
coupon-based cash payment facilities
are also available, ensuring an inclusive and seamless experience for all.
Further, A market opportunity should not end when a Mela closes. Digital channels can help enterprises reach customers beyond the event and across geographical boundaries. The SARAS ecosystem, therefore, combines physical Melas with the
SARAS Gallery
and
e-commerce channels
. The
eSARAS
platform
provides an online route for customers to discover and purchase products made by SHG entrepreneurs. This extends the market-access approach beyond face-to-face sales and can help products remain visible after the Mela.
A dedicated
SARAS Mela Digital App
was introduced in
2025
. It supports SHG nominations, attendance management, and the sharing of event-related information.  Together, physical events and digital channels offer complementary routes to market. The SARAS Mela creates direct contact with customers and buyers. Online channels can help extend product discovery and sales beyond the event.
Taking National Market Access to the Regions
The Vijayawada National SARAS Mela represents an expansion of the market-access platform into a new region. Organising national events in different locations can bring them closer to local consumers, buyers and institutional partners. It can also help producers from different States gain exposure to wider markets. This approach supports the broader objectives of DAY-NRLM and the Lakhpati Didi initiative. Women need sustainable livelihoods, but they also need ways to improve product value and expand sales. Platforms that combine selling, learning, and institutional connections can contribute to that process.
This National SARAS Mela (outside the Delhi NCR region) is a landmark initiative taken by the Government during the
SEVA Pakhwada beginning from 2nd October
2026. SARAS Melas also promote the vision of
Vocal for Local
and
Atmanirbhar Bharat
. They give consumers a direct way to discover rural products and meet the women entrepreneurs behind them. They create opportunities to preserve traditional skills while strengthening women-led enterprises. At its heart, the National SARAS Mela is about the
women behind every product, craft, and enterprise
, and the journey
from
skill to enterprise, enterprise to market, and market to sustainable livelihood.

title: 14th India Chem 2026 to Bring Global Chemicals and Petrochemicals Industry Together in Mumbai from October 22
subtitle:
Union Minister for Chemicals and Fertilizers & Health and Family Welfare Shri JP Nadda will inaugurate the event at Mumbai tomorrow

Under the theme “Advantage Bharat: An Emerging Global Chemicals Hub”, the three-day event will showcase India’s industrial capabilities, investment opportunities and emerging technologies

​​​​​​​Japan will participate as a partner country in 14th India Chem 2026
ministry: Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers :Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                21 OCT 2026 2:40PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Government of India, in partnership with the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), will organize the
14th edition of India Chem 2026 from October 22 to 24, 2026, at Bombay Exhibition Centre, NESCO, Mumbai
.
The flagship biennial event will bring together policymakers, global industry leaders, investors, technology providers, researchers and other stakeholders to explore opportunities for collaboration, trade and investment in India’s chemicals and petrochemicals sector.
The theme of the 14th edition of the event is
“Advantage Bharat: An Emerging Global Chemicals Hub,”
India Chem 2026 will feature an international exhibition and conference, positioning the event as a major platform for showcasing India’s industrial capabilities, technological advancements and potential as a global manufacturing and sourcing destination.
Union Minister for Chemicals and Fertilizers & Health and Family Welfare Shri JP Nadda will inaugurate the event
.
Union Minister of State for Chemicals
and Fertilizers & Health and Family Welfare Shrimati Anupriya Patel will grace the occasion.
Chief Minister of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha as well as senior officers from Central and State Governments will also attend the event.
Indian chemical industry poised for significant growth
India is the sixth-largest producer of chemicals in the world and the fourth-largest in Asia, provided this position the 14th India Chem 2026 holds great significance.
The Indian chemical industry is projected to reach
USD 300 billion by 2030 and USD 1 trillion by 2040
, with significant growth being witnessed. The sector’s growth potential is supported by rising demand, export opportunities, a demographic dividend, relatively low per capita consumption and enabling government initiatives.
India’s emergence as a preferred global destination is being supported by governance reforms, world-class infrastructure, robust trade and investment policies, a strong regulatory framework and the availability of skilled labour at competitive costs. The chemicals and petrochemicals sector are expected to play an important role in strengthening domestic manufacturing, expanding global value-chain participation and supporting India’s long-term economic aspirations.
Strong international participation expected
India Chem 2026 is expected to witness participation from
more than 100 countries
, including Japan, the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, countries across the European Union, Latin America, Vietnam, Korea and ASEAN nations.
Japan will participate as a partner country in 14th India Chem 2026. It is significant for the strengthening of India- Japan economic cooperation.
M
ore than 200 Indian and international exhibitors
, over
8,000 business visitors from India and abroad
, and more than
50 leading CEOs from India and overseas
at the Global CEOs Forum. Buyers’ delegations from South America, the United States, the European Union, Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries, West Europe, the Middle East, and South and Southeast Asia are also expected.
States with Petroleum, Chemicals and Petrochemicals Investment Regions (PCPIRs) and chemical hubs—including Gujarat, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Maharashtra—will showcase their capabilities and investment opportunities.
Showcasing technologies across the chemicals value chain
The exhibition will cover a wide range of products, technologies and services across chemicals, petrochemicals, process plant machinery and equipment.
The chemicals segment will feature fine and specialty chemicals, agrochemicals and fertilizers, basic chemicals, dyes and pigments, green and sustainable chemicals, pharmaceutical ingredients, water-treatment chemicals, construction chemicals and industrial research and innovation.
The petrochemicals segment will showcase polymers and engineering plastics, olefins, synthetic fibres, elastomers, aromatics and derivatives, bio-based and recycled petrochemicals, performance plastics, composite materials and specialty polymers for the automotive, aerospace and electronics sectors.
The process plant machinery and equipment segment will highlight advanced machinery, process technologies, engineering and project services, digitalisation, automation, smart manufacturing, environmental and pollution-control systems, filtration and separation technologies, laboratory equipment, analytical instruments, robotics and AI-driven solutions for chemical plants.
14th India Chem 2026  : Diverse business opportunities
14th India Chem 2026 will open avenues for technology transfer, joint ventures, contract research and manufacturing, custom synthesis, investment in PCPIRs and chemical parks, and global sourcing from India. It will also facilitate partnerships in specialty and high-performance materials, including nanomaterials, semiconductors, composites and biodegradable polymers.
Other areas of opportunity include green and sustainable technologies, bio-based chemicals, recycling and the circular economy, environmental, social and governance (ESG) solutions, safety and compliance, start-up incubation, skill development, supply-chain and logistics services, and digital platforms for business-to-business trade.
By bringing together industry, government, investors, academia and technology providers, India Chem 2026 aims to strengthen business linkages, encourage innovation and promote investment in a sector that is central to India’s manufacturing ecosystem.
Building on the legacy of India Chem
The previous edition, India Chem 2024, recorded participation from
72 countries
, with 172 exhibitors, 78 global CEOs, 135 eminent speakers, 689 foreign delegates, 1,115 Indian delegates and 8,720 business visitors. The 13th edition of India Chem registered footfall of over 15000 visitors in this prestigious B2B event. It also featured 20 state delegations showcasing investment opportunities.
Building on this participation, the 14th edition seeks to deepen international engagement, expand business partnerships and highlight India’s growing role in the global chemicals and petrochemicals industry.
India Chem 2026 will serve as a key forum for advancing the vision of
“Advantage Bharat: An Emerging Global Chemicals Hub”
by connecting global expertise with India’s manufacturing strengths, investment potential and commitment to sustainable industrial development.
